explanations.answer: The LORD God of Israel has entered through it
explanations.explanation: The reason is sitting right in verse 2: “…because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it.” Then comes the last line: “Therefore it will remain shut.” No construction crew, no battle, just the fact that He came through that gate. Friend, that's the whole reason, and the text gives it plainly.

explanations.answer: Its doors were never finished being built
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, because a shut door can mean somebody's still working on it, like a bakery with the oven off and a ladder in the doorway. But nothing in these verses says a word about building. The LORD gives the reason Himself: “…because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it.” So this gate isn't shut because it's unfinished.

explanations.answer: Enemies once broke into the city through it
explanations.explanation: A shut gate makes you picture a break-in, I know. But these verses never mention enemies. What the LORD says is that the gate stays shut “…because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it.” That's the whole reason the text gives, so we stick with it.

The prince it is. Verse 3 says, “Only the prince himself may sit inside the gateway to eat in the presence of the LORD.” He comes in by the portico of the gateway and goes out the same way. A shut gate with exactly one name on the guest list, friend.

The high priest is a fair guess, since this is a temple scene. But the verse names someone else: “Only the prince himself may sit inside the gateway to eat in the presence of the LORD.” The high priest isn't mentioned in these verses at all. The prince gets that seat.

I can see why a whole group of elders sounds right. But the verse says “Only the prince himself…” and that word “himself” keeps the list very short. No elders get mentioned in these verses. One prince, one spot in the gateway, eating in the presence of the LORD.

Facedown is right. Ezekiel the prophet looked, saw the glory of the LORD filling His temple, and says, “…I fell facedown.” That's what he did when he saw it. Friend, the glory fills the temple, and down he goes.

Asleep would be a strange way to meet this moment, friend. Ezekiel the prophet looked and saw the glory of the LORD filling His temple. Then verse 4 says he fell facedown, which is a different thing from a nap.

Backward is how I go when I trip over a rolling pin, so I understand the guess. But Ezekiel the prophet doesn't fall that way. After seeing the glory of the LORD filling His temple, he says, “…I fell facedown.”

explanations.answer: All the laws of the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD tells Ezekiel to listen closely to “…everything I tell you concerning all the statutes and laws of the house of the LORD.” He also says to take careful note of the entrance to the temple and all the exits of the sanctuary. He asks Ezekiel to look carefully with his eyes and listen closely with his ears.

explanations.answer: The names of every priest in Israel
explanations.explanation: Memorizing every priest's name would be a big job, friend. But the LORD doesn't ask for that here. What Ezekiel is to take in is “…everything I tell you concerning all the statutes and laws of the house of the LORD.”

explanations.answer: The songs sung in the temple courts
explanations.explanation: Songs would make a nice answer, but this verse doesn't mention any. The LORD points Ezekiel to something else: “…everything I tell you concerning all the statutes and laws of the house of the LORD.” Eyes and ears are for the laws, plus the entrance and the exits of the sanctuary.

explanations.answer: Foreigners uncircumcised in heart and flesh
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “…you brought in foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh to occupy My sanctuary…” Notice He says both heart and flesh. That's on top of all their other abominations.

Baal priests sound like a natural guess, but this verse never mentions them or Samaria. The LORD's words are: “…you brought in foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh to occupy My sanctuary…” So the answer comes straight from what He says.

explanations.answer: Soldiers sent by the king of Babylon
explanations.explanation: Soldiers would make this sound like an invasion. But the LORD doesn't say that here, and Babylon isn't mentioned in these verses. He says Israel itself brought in “…foreigners uncircumcised in both heart and flesh to occupy My sanctuary…”

I'd flip that one over, friend, because it's the other way around. God says, “And you have not kept charge of My holy things, but have appointed others to keep charge of My sanctuary for you.” So the house of Israel did not keep charge of them themselves. They handed the job to others.

That's right. God says, “And you have not kept charge of My holy things, but have appointed others to keep charge of My sanctuary for you.” So Israel didn't keep charge of the holy things themselves. They appointed others to do it.

True, and the verse leaves no gap. The Lord GOD says, “No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary…” Then He adds that this includes even a foreigner who lives among the Israelites. Living next door doesn't change it.

I'd switch that one, friend. The Lord GOD says, “No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary…” Then He goes further and says it holds even for a foreigner who lives among the Israelites. So the statement is true as written.

Close, but it's the other way around. Right after the consequences, God says, “Yet they shall be ministers in My sanctuary…” They'll have charge of the gates of the temple and minister there. So they do serve in the sanctuary, just not everything.

Right. God says of these Levites, “Yet they shall be ministers in My sanctuary…” They will have charge of the temple gates and slaughter the burnt offerings and other sacrifices for the people. They still bear the consequences, but they're still given work to do in His sanctuary.

Priests is right. God says, “They must not approach Me to serve Me as priests…” They also can't come near any of His holy things or the most holy things. Then God says He will appoint them to keep charge of all the work for the temple (Ezekiel 44:14).
Prophets is a good guess, but that word isn't in this verse. God says, “They must not approach Me to serve Me as priests…” So the line is about the priest's service, and that's the one missing word.
Singers would be a lovely job, and I'd listen. But the verse doesn't mention singers at all. God says, “They must not approach Me to serve Me as priests…” That's the word that fills the blank.

explanations.answer: They kept charge of His sanctuary
explanations.explanation: That's the one. God says these Levitical priests, descended from Zadok, are the ones “…who kept charge of My sanctuary when the Israelites went astray from Me…” Because of that, they are to approach Him and minister before Him. They kept charge while Israel went astray.

Following idols is what God says about the Levites in verse 10, who wandered away after their idols. For the priests descended from Zadok, He says something different. They are the ones “…who kept charge of My sanctuary when the Israelites went astray from Me…”

explanations.answer: They fled the land for Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in these verses, friend. God says the priests descended from Zadok are the ones “…who kept charge of My sanctuary when the Israelites went astray from Me…” So what the text tells us they did was keep charge of the sanctuary.

True. After naming the priests descended from Zadok, God says, “They alone shall enter My sanctuary and draw near to My table to minister before Me.” That word “alone” does the work. They will keep His charge.

Not quite, friend. God says, “They alone shall enter My sanctuary and draw near to My table to minister before Me.” He's speaking about the Levitical priests descended from Zadok, so the statement is true as written.

explanations.answer: Teach the difference between holy and common
explanations.explanation: Yes. God says, “They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common…” He adds that they're to show the people how to discern between the clean and the unclean. So they serve before Him, and they also teach the people.

explanations.answer: Lead the people's songs at the feasts
explanations.explanation: That would make the feasts lively, I admit. But this verse doesn't give the priests song duty. It says, “They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common…”

explanations.answer: Copy the scrolls of the Law for every home
explanations.explanation: Copying scrolls would be some serious hand cramp, friend. But nothing in this verse says it. What God says is, “They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common…” and to show them how to discern between the clean and the unclean.

True. God says, “In any dispute, they shall officiate as judges and judge according to My ordinances.” So the priests aren't judging by their own ideas, but by His ordinances. They also keep His laws for all His appointed feasts and keep His Sabbaths holy.

Hold on, friend, it's true as written. God says, “In any dispute, they shall officiate as judges and judge according to My ordinances.” So in a dispute, the priests judge, and His ordinances set the standard.

Yes. God says, “In regard to their inheritance, I am their inheritance.” Then He says to give them no possession in Israel, “…for I am their possession.” Imagine that: no land, and God Himself as the inheritance.

Fields are what most people expect an inheritance to be. But God says, “You are to give them no possession in Israel, for I am their possession.” So no fields for the priests. Their inheritance is God Himself.

That would be a very big herd, friend. But these verses never say it. God says, “In regard to their inheritance, I am their inheritance.” and that they get no possession in Israel. They do eat from the offerings, but their inheritance is Him.

explanations.answer: So a blessing may rest on their homes
explanations.explanation: That's what verse 30 says: “You are to give your first batch of dough to the priest, so that a blessing may rest upon your homes.” That's the reason the text gives. As a cookie man, I've got a lot of respect for a first batch.

explanations.answer: So the priests can feed the poor
explanations.explanation: Feeding the poor is a kind thing, but this verse doesn't give it as the reason. It says, “You are to give your first batch of dough to the priest, so that a blessing may rest upon your homes.” The reason stated is a blessing on the homes.

explanations.answer: So the next harvest comes in early
explanations.explanation: An early harvest would be nice, but the verse never says that. It says to give the first batch of dough to the priest “…so that a blessing may rest upon your homes.” That's the reason God gives.
